TM-RF-15-001 Rev. A · C-band 6×6 array · VSWR investigation

1Executive summary

The 6×6 dual-polarised stacked-patch array radiates with the expected broadside gain, but its input match is poor: the VSWR does not stay below 3:1 across the 4–7 GHz band. Telmart analysed the design with full-wave electromagnetic simulation built directly from the supplied layout files, at element level and for the complete array.

~16 %Element bandwidth (VSWR ≤ 3), 5.35–6.26 GHz
54 %Bandwidth required for 4–7 GHz
8.7–9.8 dBiElement gain referred to accepted power: the radiator works
VSWR ≈ 9Best achievable with any feed-network match (worst case 4–7 GHz)
Root cause. The radiating element is inherently narrow-band. The edge-fed driven patch and the parasitic patch are nearly the same size and produce a single merged resonance near 5.8 GHz, instead of two separate resonances spread across the band. Outside about 5.35–6.26 GHz most of the power is reflected. That is why the gain looks correct while the VSWR is poor.
Conclusion. The problem cannot be fixed in the feed network alone. Meeting VSWR < 3 over 4–7 GHz requires a redesigned wideband radiating element. Short-term improvements (equal parasitic sizes, per-element transformers, assembly tolerances) centre and stabilise the present band but will not widen it to 4–7 GHz.
Status. The element-level analysis is complete. The full-array simulation is still running; the preliminary array results in section 5.4 agree with the element-level conclusions, and bench measurements of the built panel (section 5.6) confirm the input-match behaviour. The measurements also show a gain shortfall of about 3 dB mid-band and a strong gain drop above 6 GHz, which is now part of the investigation. A first wideband redesign iteration has been completed and has defined the requirements for the next design iteration (section 7).

3Design under review

The array uses 36 identical driven patches (17.07 mm) on a 0.8 mm RT5880 laminate. Each driven patch has a parasitic patch (16.2–17.8 mm, graded by row) on 0.4 mm FR4, held 4 mm above it by an air gap. Two independent 36-way corporate networks on the driven-patch layer feed the top/bottom edges (port 1, V-pol) and the left/right edges (port 2, H-pol) of every patch.

ParameterValue
Element pitch≈ 44 mm (0.59 λ at 4 GHz, 1.03 λ at 7 GHz)
Stack-upGround / RT5880 0.8 mm / driven patches + feeds / 4 mm air / FR4 0.4 mm / parasitic patches
Feed lines0.73 mm (100 Ω), 1.38 mm (70.7 Ω quarter-wave transformers), 2.48 mm (50 Ω)
Element feedDirect edge feed through a short 50 Ω stub, no matching section

5Findings

5.1 Element performance as built

A single element, simulated with its own feed stubs, is matched (VSWR ≤ 3) only from about 5.35 to 6.26 GHz, with a best return loss of 10.8 dB at 5.84 GHz. The element still radiates efficiently (8.7–9.8 dBi referred to accepted power), but the realised gain drops at the band edges because of the mismatch.

5.2 Diagnostic variants

VariantResultWhat it shows
Parasitic patch removedNo match anywhere in 4–7 GHzThe edge feed is not matched to the patch; the match relies entirely on the parasitic
Parasitic enlarged ×1.15 / 1.25 / 1.35Matched window moves down and becomes narrower (12 %, 4 %, none)Resizing tunes where the element works, not how wide
Parasitic graded by row (as built)Each row matched at a slightly different frequencyPart of the aperture is always mismatched

5.3 Can the feed network correct it?

The best possible passive match was computed from the simulated element impedance (any series line, quarter-wave transformer and shunt stub). The worst-case VSWR over 4–7 GHz improves only from 28.6 to about 9.4. The element's impedance varies too much across the band to be compensated by a passive network (Bode–Fano limit). The correction must be made in the radiating element.

5.4 Full array (preliminary)

The complete board, with both 36-way networks, is being simulated. Because the long feed networks ring for a long time, the run takes many hours. The preliminary results below are taken from the data recorded so far.

  • Both inputs are best in the middle of the band (about 5.0–6.2 GHz) and mostly at VSWR 3:1 or worse below ~4.8 GHz and above ~6.3 GHz, matching the element result.
  • The V/H isolation is better than 20 dB over most of the band.
  • Final array figures will be issued in the next revision of this report.
TM-RF-15-001 Rev. A · C-band 6×6 array · VSWR investigation

5.5 Wideband redesign: first iteration

To define the corrective design, an aperture-coupled stacked patch, the established route to about 50 % bandwidth, was explored in 40 full-wave simulations, including automatic optimisation. The best candidate so far is matched from 4.95 to 5.75 GHz. It is a valid design but not yet wider than the present element. The iteration identified clearly what the next design must change:

  • Patches must be printed on thin low-loss laminates over foam rather than suspended in air, so the two resonances can be separated across the band.
  • A resonant (dog-bone or H-shaped) coupling slot is needed to add a third resonance at the top of the band; H-slots also provide the second polarisation.
  • The element must be optimised in its array environment (periodic unit cell at the 44 mm pitch).

5.6 Measured results of the built panel

The client's built panel was measured on the bench: input match of both ports with a calibrated network analyser, and broadside gain by substitution against a reference horn.

f (GHz)S11 port A (dB)S11 port B (dB)Gain V (dBi)Gain H (dBi)Aperture limit (dBi)Aperture efficiency V / H

6.2-5.3-9.915.113.226.18 % / 5 %

* nearest S11 marker (5.7 / 5.9 GHz). Gain by substitution against a reference horn at ~5 m. Port A/B to V/H mapping and radome condition during the gain test to be confirmed.

  • Input match confirms the analysis. Both ports show the same rippled response as the simulated array and are best in the middle of the band. Port A meets VSWR ≤ 3 at all markers except 6.2 GHz; port B is at about VSWR 3 at 4.9–5.2 GHz.
  • Gain is below the rating. Peak gain is 20.4 dBi (V) and 20.0 dBi (H), about 3 dB under 23 dBi, corresponding to 25–35 % aperture efficiency mid-band (a well-designed panel reaches 50–70 %).
  • Gain collapses at the top of the band: 11–15 dBi at 6.2–6.4 GHz (3–8 % efficiency). Mismatch explains at most about 1.5 dB of this. The remaining shortfall points to losses or phase errors (feed network, FR4 parasitic layer, radome) and is being investigated.

7Recommendations and next steps

7.1 Corrective actions

#ActionExpected resultType
1Redesign the radiating element as a wideband dual-polarised element (aperture-coupled stacked patch on laminate/foam, or L-probe / crossed-dipole alternative)Only route to VSWR < 3 (target < 2) over 4–7 GHzRequired
2Use one parasitic size on all rows unless a taper is intendedAll rows matched at the same frequencyQuick fix
3Add a quarter-wave transformer on each element feed (edge resistance to 100 Ω)Present band centred and deeper; not widerQuick fix
4Control the 4 mm air-gap spacer tolerance (±0.1 mm)Stable, repeatable match between boardsProduction
5Reduce the pitch to ≤ 30 mm if the full band must be free of grating lobesClean patterns up to 7 GHz (needs the smaller wideband element)Design

8Assumptions and limitations

  • Bench measurements were made by the client team on a bench range (~5 m), not in an anechoic chamber; gain values carry an estimated ±1–2 dB uncertainty. The port A/B to V/H mapping and the radome condition during the gain test are to be confirmed.
  • The air gap is modelled as 4.0 mm of air (εr 1.0), as built.
  • Copper thickness, solder mask, connectors and the mechanical spacers are not modelled.
  • The array mesh (0.5 mm) approximates the 0.73 mm lines, which can shift network resonances by a few percent.
  • Full-array results in this revision are preliminary (simulation still running).
